meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A nation that destroys its soils destroys itself. Forests are the lungs of our land, purifying the air and giving fresh strength to our people'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Roosevelt words, spliced: the 'lungs' line is from 1935, the soil line from a 1937 letter to governors. No document contains the combined quote.

answer.label: Not one Franklin D. Roosevelt quote — two statements spliced together
answer.sourceLine: Both sentences are genuinely Roosevelt’s, but they come from two different documents. The “lungs” line is from his 29 January 1935 statement accepting the Schlich Forestry Medal. The soil line is from his 26 February 1937 letter to state governors, where it reads “The Nation that destroys its soil destroys itself.” No document joining the two sentences has been found, and the popular version rewords both lines slightly.

source.heading: Two real documents, no single source

docMeta.dd: Letter to all State Governors on a Uniform Soil Conservation Law (26 February 1937)
Statement on Being Awarded the Schlich Forestry Medal (29 January 1935)
The American Presidency Project (UC Santa Barbara)

source.excerpt: 1937 letter to the governors: “I need not emphasize to you the seriousness of the problem and the desirability of our taking effective action, as a Nation and in the several States, to conserve the soil as our basic asset. The Nation that destroys its soil destroys itself.” — 1935 statement to the Society of American Foresters: “The forests are also needed for mitigating extreme climatic fluctuations, holding the soil on the slopes, retaining the moisture in the ground, and controlling the equable flow of water in our streams. The forests are the ‘lungs’ of our land, purifying the air and giving fresh strength to our people. Truly, they make the country more livable.”
trail: 29 January 1935 — In a written statement addressed “To the Society of American Foresters,” accepting the Schlich Forestry Medal, Roosevelt writes: “The forests are the ‘lungs’ of our land, purifying the air and giving fresh strength to our people.” American Presidency Project ↗

26 February 1937 — In a letter to all state governors urging them to adopt the Standard State Soil Conservation Districts Law, Roosevelt writes: “The Nation that destroys its soil destroys itself.” American Presidency Project ↗

Later — The two lines are passed around as a single quote, with the soil sentence paraphrased and placed first. Wikiquote lists the combined form in its Disputed section and notes that no original document in precisely this form has been located. Wikiquote ↗
source.excerptNote: These are two separate texts, shown together only for comparison. The popular quote puts the 1937 sentence first, changes “The Nation … soil” to “A nation … soils,” and, in the forests sentence, drops the opening “The” and the quotation marks Roosevelt put around “lungs.”

author.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
author.heading: About Franklin D. Roosevelt
author.bio: Franklin Delano Roosevelt was president of the United States from 1933 until his death in 1945. He led the country through the Great Depression and the Second World War. His New Deal included major conservation programs, among them the federal soil-erosion work of the Soil Conservation Service. Both genuine sentences behind this quote come from that conservation push.

misattribution.heading: Real words, wrong shape
misattribution.intro: The popular quote names the right person, but it isn’t one quote. It joins sentences from two separate Roosevelt documents and rewords one of them.

items.who: Franklin D. Roosevelt, as a single statement
items.why: No Roosevelt document joining both sentences has been located. Wikiquote lists the combined form under Disputed: it “approximates 2 separate statements of FDR,” but “no original document in precisely this form” has been located. Wikiquote ↗

items.scope: “A nation that destroys its soils destroys itself”
items.why: In the letter to the governors the sentence reads “The Nation that destroys its soil destroys itself”: The, not A, and soil, not soils. Letter of 26 February 1937 ↗

items.scope: “Forests are the lungs of our land”
items.why: This sentence comes from Roosevelt’s statement accepting the Schlich Forestry Medal from the Society of American Foresters. It predates the soil letter, and it reads “The forests are the ‘lungs’ of our land,” with “lungs” in quotation marks. Statement of 29 January 1935 ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Roosevelt wrote “The forests are the ‘lungs’ of our land, purifying the air and giving fresh strength to our people” on 29 January 1935, and “The Nation that destroys its soil destroys itself” on 26 February 1937. No document that joins the two sentences has been found. Wikiquote ↗

context.heading: Why the lines were written
lead: The soil sentence closes the opening paragraph of Roosevelt’s 26 February 1937 letter to every state governor. The letter pointed to “the dust storms and floods of the last few years” and asked each state to pass the Standard State Soil Conservation Districts Law. That model law let local “soil conservation districts” carry out erosion control. Read the letter ↗

The forests sentence is from an earlier and separate text: Roosevelt’s written thanks to the Society of American Foresters for its Schlich Forestry Medal. In it he argues that “the preservation of the forests must be lifted above mere dollars and cents considerations.” Read the statement ↗

sourcesVerified.claim: FDR's letter to all state governors, dated February 26, 1937, contains the sentence 'The Nation that destroys its soil destroys itself.' It also cites dust storms and floods and urges states to adopt the Standard State Soil Conservation Districts Law. The letter does not contain 'forests' or 'lungs'.

FDR's statement 'To the Society of American Foresters' accepting the Schlich Forestry Medal, dated January 29, 1935, contains 'The forests are the "lungs" of our land, purifying the air and giving fresh strength to our people.' and 'The preservation of the forests must be lifted above mere dollars and cents considerations.' It does not contain 'destroys its soil'.

Wikiquote's FDR page lists the combined quote in its Disputed section and says it approximates two separate FDR statements (26 February 1937 and 29 January 1935), with no original document in precisely this form located. Its sourced 1930s entry notes the 1937 statement has been paraphrased and prefixed to the 1935 statement. Checked via the raw wikitext: the entry sits between ==Disputed== and {{Disputed end}}.
The Society of American Foresters' Sir William Schlich Memorial Award dates from 1935.
Franklin D. Roosevelt was born January 30, 1882 and died April 12, 1945.
